name: Untitled Epic of Gilgamesh graphic novel by Robert Macfarlane, Johnny Flynn and Dave McKean (final title not yet announced as of September 2026) [uncertain]
date: Acquisition announced 13 March 2024 (London Book Fair, Day Two; The Bookseller and Bleeding Cool, both 13-14 March 2024). Publication scheduled for spring 2027 by Hamish Hamilton (Penguin). Not yet published as of September 2026, so no firm date, ISBN or page count is public [uncertain]
creator: Robert Macfarlane (nature writer, Cambridge fellow; The Old Ways, Landmarks, Underland, Is a River Alive?), Johnny Flynn (actor and folk musician, Johnny Flynn & The Sussex Wit) and Dave McKean (artist, director of MirrorMask and Luna, long-time Neil Gaiman collaborator). Acquired for UK and Commonwealth rights by Simon Prosser, publishing director of Hamish Hamilton
form: Graphic novel with a dual narrative: one strand retells the epic (Gilgamesh and Enkidu's journey to the Sacred Cedar Wood), the second follows George Smith, the self-taught British Museum engraver who deciphered the Flood tablet in 1872. The outline also notes a forward-looking coda [uncertain: not confirmed in accessible sources]
translator_access: None of the three reads Akkadian or Sumerian; this is an adaptation, not a translation. Which scholarly translation(s) they work from has not been disclosed [uncertain]. The earlier Macfarlane/Flynn album drew on the epic generally without naming a crib.
versions_used: Not disclosed [uncertain]. The Smith strand implies attention to the Nineveh Standard Babylonian tablets (Smith worked on the Ashurbanipal library fragments, Tablet XI in particular). Emphasis on the Cedar Wood suggests the Humbaba episode (Tablets II-V) is central; whether the 2011 Sulaymaniyah Tablet V fragment, with its noisy living forest, is used is unknown
non_standard_material: Unknown until publication [uncertain]. Structurally, the book frames the ancient text with a second, modern narrative (Smith), so the recovery of the poem itself is dramatised rather than footnoted
gap_policy: Unknown until publication [uncertain]. The 'tale of the tale' structure gives the book a natural way to show gaps as physical breaks in clay, since Smith's own story turns on a missing fragment
typography_of_absence: Unknown [uncertain]. McKean's mixed-media collage style (photography, paint, found texture) makes a visual rendering of broken tablets plausible, but no pages have been released
turning_point: Not yet knowable [uncertain]. Announcement copy stresses the journey to the Sacred Cedar Wood, and the precursor album Lost in the Cedar Wood (2021) treats the felling of the forest as the key moral event. Flynn described the story as 'the arrogance of man in nature' in which 'Gilgamesh is chased down by his sense of mortality' (American Songwriter, 2021), suggesting the forest killing and its consequence (Enkidu's death) as the hinge
arc_interpretation: Likely ecological as well as elegiac [uncertain]. The precursor project read the epic through the pandemic: Macfarlane sent Flynn 'articles about deforestation being the root of the pandemic', and Flynn called the poem an 'alternative to the creation myth, a different take on The Garden of Eden' about 'love, and of course, loss' (American Songwriter, 2021). Adding George Smith turns the arc into a second story about recovery and reading, and a forward-looking coda (per the outline note) would push the ending past Uruk's walls toward the present or future
key_passages: No pages released; renderings of Shamhat and Enkidu, Siduri, the Tablet XI bedchamber line and the walls of Uruk are unknown [uncertain]. The album offers proxies: tracks 'Enkidu Walked' and 'Tree Rings' draw directly on the epic
diction_and_metre: Unknown [uncertain]. Expect Macfarlane's compressed, word-rich prose (he is known for reviving landscape vocabulary) and possibly song-like text from Flynn; the album used folk ballad forms
sample_line: No line from the book is public. Closest available is Simon Prosser's description that it will 'tell both the tale, then, and the tale of the tale' (The Bookseller / Bleeding Cool, March 2024) [uncertain]
critical_response: None yet; the book is unpublished. The precursor album Lost in the Cedar Wood (Transgressive, 14 May 2021) scored 76 on Metacritic; NME gave 4/5 and Clash 8/10
regional_reception: None; UK and Commonwealth rights only announced, no Arabic or Kurdish edition or Iraqi engagement reported [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: No machine involvement. The project puts a human decipherer at the centre of the retelling: George Smith, a working-class engraver who taught himself cuneiform in the British Museum, is the Victorian counterpart of today's AI fragment-matching and sign-recognition work (e.g. the Fragmentarium). The book dramatises the reading of clay as a human act of obsession and luck, just as machines take over parts of that job. McKean has also spoken publicly against generative AI imagery (Creative Bloq, calling on artists to 'revolt against the soulless machines'), which makes the book a pointed piece of hand-made craft
essay_hooks: (1) 'both the tale, then, and the tale of the tale' (Simon Prosser, Hamish Hamilton, March 2024): a ready-made frame for an essay about retelling and recovery. (2) George Smith, 'the auto-didact, working-class genius who in the 1860s taught himself to read the ancient cuneiform script' (announcement copy), set against machine sign recognition now. (3) Born in lockdown: Macfarlane and Flynn wrote Lost in the Cedar Wood over WhatsApp in 2020, reading the Cedar Forest through deforestation and the pandemic (American Songwriter; Wikipedia). (4) Dave McKean, one of the most AI-sceptical artists in comics, drawing the oldest story on record (Creative Bloq). (5) Due spring 2027, so it can be cited as the next retelling on the way
